utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided to sit this morning in the absence of Judge Kamenova. We consider it in the interests of justice to continue. She is absent for personal reasons. We can now go into closed session to enable the witness to come into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Tanic. You can hear me, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you want to deal with the issue of whether or not the witness should be invited again to give the identification of personnel with whom he worked, or do you wish to proceed first with your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was prepared to do either one. It may help if I ask him some questions first that will assist me with my arguments about least one of those points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think also that when we do have the discussion on that matter, we should do so in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, the evidence will now continue. Mr. Hannis will have a chance to re-examine you. Again, please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to tell the truth continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tanic. I want to start by asking you some questions related to the topic of NATO target information; and in paragraph 117 of your statement where you indicate you personally passed on to Milosevic information, you also say: "This information was also included in an official memo on NATO targets sent by the SDB to Milosevic." My question is: When you say "this information," do you mean the information that you had, or do you mean general information that the SDB had from sources other than you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean my sources, but I would not be surprised if other information from other sources had been added to that. But I primarily meant my own sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly then, this official memo contained the information that you had provided from your western source?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 118 you mention -- well, you say: "I know from my SDB contacts," which you have told us previously in response to a question from Mr. Ackerman, were the ones where we've been calling number 1 and 2 that you named in closed session. "I know from my SDB contacts that the SDB provided Milosevic with maximum information about future targets, which they received from western friends in good-will in order to avoid civilian casualties." Regarding that "maximum information about future targets," were you the source of that information, or are you indicating that number 1 and number 2 got other information about targets from western sources?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was other information apart from the information I provided, in particularly when it came to potential civilian casualties in the vicinity of military targets or in civilian facilities that were now used for military purposes. And as far as I understand, there was some understanding in the NATO alliance for any leaks of information regarding potential civilian casualties. This was not espionage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... received and provided about the RTS television station. Was that the only target information that you had passed on, or was there other?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was other information, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall now any of the specifics regarding the other targeting information you passed on? Are we talking about two or 20 or 200 targets?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As you know, NATO divided its air campaign in three stages; one, two, and three. And I had certain targets revealed to me in all those stages, primarily related to potential civilian casualties, but also some that regarding -- that had to do with military targets; and, of course, this was much more strictly kept military secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give me any rough estimate of how many that would total? You received some information regarding each of the three stages, but any idea of the total number of targets we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I want to go to the topic of the tape-recording that you described having opportunity to listen to portions of that purport to be between Mr. Sainovic and General Lukic. I think you testified yesterday at page 85, line 21, that you didn't recognise the voices. Was there anything, however, about the content of the portions of the conversation you heard that was inconsistent with that being a conversation between Lukic and Sainovic, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Speculative, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I think that's a perfectly reasonable question to ask in the circumstances. I repel that objection. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I really couldn't recognise them because I don't know their voices, but there was nothing in there that would be not something that they would not be talking about. I said yesterday that I couldn't authenticate the tape, and I can just confirm that the tapes existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I -- I know yesterday, at one point in time, I think it was you or maybe Mr. Lukic pointed out, that we had made a mistake in the transcript. It was initially written down as Vracar, V-r-a-c-a-r, when it was actually Racak that you were speaking of. But I note that at -- the last time I checked at page 78, lines 5 and lines 17, we still had Vracar. In all cases regarding that tape, are you talking about Racak?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents that I could hear and the way I remember it, it pertained to Racak because it was mentioned. But the contents are really quite hazy in my memory right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now go to a question Mr. Ackerman asked you on -- yesterday at page 55, line 11. You pointed out that when you testified in Milosevic you indicated that you had not requested any name change or move. But since you testified in Milosevic, you actually have been put in the witness protection programme. You have gone to a new country and received a new identity. Did anything happen after your testimony that caused you to you change your mind about whether you wanted or needed a new identity?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he said yesterday that what happened was that he had been kidnapped, and that's what changed his mind. So I think that's what Mr. Hannis is fishing for, and he's already given the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not what I'm fishing for, Your Honour. He was kidnapped before he testified. I'm asking if something happened after he testified that changed his mind, because he said in May 2002 he didn't want it. Since then he has apparently changed his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I repel that objection. Carry on, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The key decision for me to accept a new identity, together with my wife and for us to start a new life from scratch, was based on when I spoke to Mihajlovic in Paris, I mean Dusan Mihajlovic. I realised that it was absolutely not possible for me to get my property back, to have some kind of reasonable way of life in the country. Until then, I had hoped that this would be resolved in some way, but then I realised that there was not a chance of that, and the degree of threat was the same as it was during the Milosevic regime. So this was the key element. Before that, I had sent him a few faxes, asking him to solve all those problems with the units for especially operations and -- regarding my property, but nothing -- nothing happened. I couldn't even get my books back, the books that belonged to me and my wife that had been stolen. So this was what actually made me decide. And when I testified in the Milosevic case, I was already in the witness protection programme, but I noted that I had not asked that before the testimony -- before I gave evidence. When I met with the OTP investigators, I had hoped that I would be able to be able to go on living under my identity, but unfortunately that didn't work out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in Paris, when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was in 2001 or early 2002, about six months before I gave evidence in the case against Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's described in Mr. Mijatovic's book, isn't it? He writes about it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- this meeting is described in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at page 50, line 7 from yesterday, Mr. Ackerman was asking you about New Democracy and the elections in September of 1997. Do you recall exactly when New Democracy left the coalition? Did that happen before the elections? At the time of the elections? After the elections?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the elections. We simply were not on the same slate as we had been until then. Our list was SPS, JUL, New Democracy, Slobodan Milosevic. We simply did not accept Milosevic's invitation to join in again. We prepared our own platform, Mr. Mihajlovic and I drafted it. We presented the main arguments for our rift, and we adopted this platform, and then we parted ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you go about leaving the coalition? I'm not clear on how that worked. Did your party make some kind of announcement or have a press conference, or did you just walk out of the building? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We simply were not put on the slate for the new elections, and we had decided that at the session of our Main Board, that we should go to the elections alone and not in coalition with Mr. Milosevic. And the main reason was the reason I described earlier, our disagreement on his Kosovo policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess my question is: Did your party convey that information to Mr. Milosevic, that you no longer wanted to be part of the coalition?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us when and how that was done.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was done in a face-to-face meeting between Milosevic and Mihajlovic. I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let me ask you one more question about targeting, that I forgot to ask earlier. You mentioned that the SDB was also obtaining information from western sources, other than simply through you. Do you know or did anyone tell you whether or not Mr. Milosevic was receiving that information?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely certain he received this information because, first of all, I cannot imagine how he wouldn't receive them; and secondly, what SDB did was, regardless of the level of the operatives, it all fed straight to the top; and then Rade Markovic relayed this information to Milosevic. It is absolutely certain that Mr. Milosevic had at his disposal all the information relevant that could shorten the war, reduce the casualties. As far as I know, there were several credible sources, so I don't want to claim all the credit. I spoke about myself here, and that's why I keep says "I," "I," but there were other credible sources that provided this kind of information to the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I understand your answer correctly, you seem certain that he did receive that information because it should have worked that way, but did anybody tell you that he had received that information? Did anybody in SDB say, Yes, yes, he knows, or are you just assuming based on how things worked in the SDB?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on several occasions, number 2 - whom we mentioned closed session - told me that this was going to Radonjic and Rade and directly on to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you aware of any event or situation that would indicate Mr. Milosevic had received information about targeting and had taken some action based on that information?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the facilities in Belgrade where there could be civilian casualties, some measures were taken primarily as regards the house where the -- the building where his daughter had her radio station and the republican MUP was evacuated. But I think that they did it on their own initiative; they did not wait for his say so. Some of the civilian targets in Belgrade that should have been evacuated had not been; and as regard the military targets, I was not on the ground and I had nothing to do with the military targets, so I cannot give you my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now go to Wednesday, the 15th of November, Mr. Ackerman was asking you about your SDB sources, and I think the page 69, line 1 - I'm sorry I don't have the current four-digit number - Judge Bonomy was asking about your SDB sources. And you mentioned that: "A lot of other individuals over a number of years in the SDB" were persons that you had dealings with. But you've told us that basically your four sources were Zoran Mijatovic, Jovica Stanisic, and source 1 and 2, who you named in closed session. Those four persons of the information that you've passed on to us in your report and your testimony, what percentage of your information came from those four sources, as opposed to the "lot of other individuals over the years?" Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The largest percentage came from those four persons. As for the strategic information, Zoran Mijatovic provided vast majority of it and number 1 would relay his information or the information from Mr. Stanisic when we're talking about strategic information, the attitude towards JUL, problems in the domestic situation, the so-called internal enemy, problems in foreign relations, the exchange of information between the Serbian and British intelligence services that took place three times. The first time was in 1994, then in 1997, and I don't recall the third time when it was. Every time it happened through me and the gentleman whose name is not mentioned here. This means that both services knew who I was; and because I was not in espionage, I could function there in this channel. And of course primarily Kosovo, how to prevent the war in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Hannis could assist. He -- the transcript, page 69, line 1, has nothing to do with the question he asked. Mr. Lukic was cross-examining at that point, so I'm wondering where, if he knows, in the transcript that this came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know the quote was based on a question that you had asked, and the witness had given an answer about a lot of other individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because you've attributed the issue arising to Mr. Ackerman, he's anxious to know where in the transcript that is, I think, so that he can check it. Can you help, since apparently page 69 is during Mr. Lukic's cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It appears that it's on page 6682, that answer about a number of individuals -- I'm sorry, it is Mr. Lukic who is speaking at that time, and I apologise to both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think your answer then did indicate that the vast majority of your strategic information came from Mr. Mijatovic. And with regard to the information you got from your SDB sources, you told us about seeing rules of procedure or operation for police, and you told us about the tape purporting to be a conversation between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lukic. Did the SDB also provide you information in the forms of any other kinds of documents, or was it all simply orally communicated to you by your sources?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, it was orally communicated. The SDB is not in the habit of providing documents. On very rare occasions, they simply show you documents. They don't let you take them home if you need to check something or compare things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we could bring up Exhibit 2481.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I do believe this was Mr. Ackerman. He was talking to you about the -- I think it's your -- your inference that Mr. Milosevic's speech, in June 1997, undoing the agreement that you and others had tried to negotiate with the Kosovo Albanians. Exhibit 2481 is the jointly agreed positions, which I think you testified to earlier as being those that came out of a meeting in New York. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in your statement at paragraph 32, you indicate that you and Fehmi Agani had initially agreed on these terms as far back as 1995.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, generally speaking, yes, because the Albanian side had really been knocked down, and they had to adopt a much softer position after the Dayton peace. Albanian policy in Kosovo was at that time not friendly, but they were willing to give way to a greater extent. We had to make sure that negotiations got started without any preconditions attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is paragraph 2 of that document entitled, "Jointly Agreed Positions" the reflection of how you tried to resolve that thorny issue of Kosovo's status or independence or secession by having both sides agree that there weren't going to be any preconceived positions or preconditions?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is stated clearly in point 2 that the problem can only be solved through dialogue and mutual agreement with no preconditions or prejudgement of possible outcomes, and point 3 compliments this. But it was not me who created this agreement; it was arrived at step by step. Every two or three months, we would get a little closer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object to that. His direct evidence -- his direct evidence on this is that point 2 means that the agreement -- the Kosovo Albanian agreement was to step back from independence; that's his direct evidence. This is re-examination; this isn't appropriate to ask the witness to change his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure those two things are inconsistent, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They may be, Mr. Hannis. The problem is it's a leading question, and the answer really is of little value in view of the nature of the question I think. My recollection of the evidence, the initial evidence, was that paragraph 2 was interpreted by the witness as something different from what its actual contents on the face of it -- on the face of them mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and he does make a statement about paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can't be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can't be undone, Mr. O'Sullivan, but your point is well made and will be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to another topic, Mr. Tanic. This is from Tuesday, the 14th. You were being questioned about your -- when you were seized off the street; your kidnapping, as you've described it. Why, if you know, did your captors let you go? Why did they release you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were three reasons. The first was pure luck, because they released us only two or three hours after the unsuccessful attempt to assassinate Vuk Draskovic on the Ibar main road. As my wife and I were abducted in the course of the day, of course, this became known in Belgrade, because very arrogantly they sealed off the entire neighbourhood and kidnapped first her then me. Then they attempted to assassinate Vuk Draskovic on the Ibarski main road, and I think they found it inconvenient to deal with us at the same time, so they wanted to get rid of us. I think that's the first reason. The second reason is that intending to protect my life and the life of my wife, I left them in the conviction that some things might be completed; this had to do with the British intelligence service. And thirdly, they were confused because they had received contradictory orders. They appeared to be confused. They said, "Look, this is a British spy. Kill him. Beat him." And then in the course of their investigation, it turned out -- well, I can't say we were comrades, but it turned out we were on the same side at least when normal things -- where normal things are concerned. So when you add up all these three elements I think they all contributed to our release. But I think the first element is the assassination attempt because they arrived all in a sweat, and they were in a great hurry to get rid of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to the second item you mentioned in that answer, were they requesting you try to do something in connection with the British secret service; and if so, what was that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They tried to pretend that all this beating was a test, to show how strong I was physically and psychologically, that they wanted to establish contact with the British intelligence services through me, and to defect, to oppose, the Milosevic regime. But this seemed a little bit like science fiction. But this possibility was left open to see whether they were sincere, but in fact it transpired that they were trying to trap the British intelligence services, together with representatives to come to Serbia or Macedonia, and then to arrest them all and to put us all in prison. I'm sure it was a came they were trying to play. When they couldn't get anything out of me through beating and torture, they tried to trick me. That was my understanding of this event, although I don't know, of course, what was on their minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. When Mr. Fila was questioning you on Tuesday of this week, he was asking you about tape-recordings. At page 6527, line 13, you said: "Everything was taped during the war." With regard to that, can you tell us what agency or agencies were tape-recording people; and particularly, what agencies would have been tape-recording Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lukic -- General Lukic, I should say, rather than counsel Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intercepting communications, wire-tapping, those are normal methods used in wartime, and they were used in our case. They tried to see what they could get. The SDB did those things, as did the foreigners, of course. I can't say there were any special targets. Some people were of interest to the security services and these were monitored. But in general, they were just recording everything to see what they could find.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... anything about where those tapes are stored or where the archives are maintained relating to those kinds of materials?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I want to go to the 14th of this month, Tuesday. I think it was Mr. O'Sullivan was questioning you, at this point in time, about paragraph 108 of your written statement, where you had indicated you had a heated conversation with Mr. Milosevic about the NATO bombing and his claim about the need to have enough civilian casualties to influence public opinion regarding NATO's bombing. I would like to go through this again and see if I have it clear. Did you speak one-to-one with Mr. Milosevic about this?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you also hear him on a speaker-phone with Vuk Draskovic talking about this?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to say that Mr. Draskovic later denied having that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Regarding that conversation, though, I believe you indicated -- well, tell me, were other persons present when that conversation occurred that you overheard on the speaker-phone? Anyone else present or listening in, other than Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Draskovic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The others were in the next room while we had a light lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what building did this take place in?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the seat of our party in a villa in -- oh, god, I've started forgetting street names. It was a villa in the centre of town, the headquarters of New Democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you mentioned at the beginning of your testimony, on that day, a book by Predrag Simic. Can you tell us who Mr. Simic is or was.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Simic was the managing director of the Institute of Strategic Studies established by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He was the director of that institute. Later on, because of some disagreements, he became an associate; and after the fall of the Milosevic regime, he became one of the advisors of the new president, Mr. Kostunica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on any further with that, Mr. Hannis, allow me to ask one thing more of the witness. The face-to-face brief discussion about the need for civilian casualties and the speaker-phone conversation, did they occur on different days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- oh, yes, yes. Yes, on two different days. Yes, excuse me, on two different days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember roughly how far apart they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe two or three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to follow-up on that, do you recall which one occurred first?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's quite difficult for me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to Mr. Simic, do you know the name of the book he wrote that dealt with -- well, with you and the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It dealt with the negotiations, and I was mentioned in it. The title of the book is: "The Road to Rambouillet."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness. I have an excerpt from that book which we've disclosed to the Defence, and I would propose to submit to you later on, once we've loaded it into e-court pertaining to Mr. Tanic's participation in the negotiations he's talked about. And with that, I'm ready to discuss the other if the Court desires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the appropriate way to deal with this to actually put to the witness the extract and ask him if it's consistent with his recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I've thought about that doing that, if that's agreeable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How lengthy is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- I have three -- three separate extracts that total maybe two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And has he already given evidence in relation to all of these references? I don't mean about -- I don't mean in the context of the book. Does each of the references deal with something he's already given evidence about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's 11 pages in the B/C/S. It's ERN K053-6040 through 6051 that we provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does anyone have an objection to that being exhibited? No. Very well. We'll just exhibit it without following the course I suggested, since the witness has had a chance to deal with the matters referred to in that. You'll need to deal by e-mail with confirmation of a number for that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you. I don't know if the Court wants to have questions for the witness, or if we want to send him out and discuss the revolving -- involving the three unidentified sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment, Mr. Hannis. We'll go into closed session while the witness leaves the courtroom. Mr. Tanic, we are going to deal with a matter of law, and while we do that you should remain outside the courtroom and then you'll return when we've made a decision.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I need to wait. The translators said yesterday these make too much noise. Your Honour, I have very little to say. I think I have made my position very clear yesterday on more than one occasion. The only issue that came up this morning from what Mr. Hannis said I think was his uncertainty about the meaning of contumacious. And I don't think there's any uncertainty about the meaning of contumacious at all. If the Court orders somebody to do something and they say: "No," that's contumacious. So if you say to the Witness, Mr. Witness, would you answer the question, and he says, I decline. I don think that's contempt wish to do so. But when you order him to do so, and he declines, then it is. He hasn't justification for doing that and that is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you're quite right on that and that seems to be the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, which I think has established in only the one -- well, there may be more than one case now, but a case in which I was involved. There is the earlier question, though, whether the order to answer the question ought to be made. And it's to that really that Mr. Hannis's argument applies properly. In other words, is there a good national security interest to justify the Bench declining to accept your invitation to order him to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the matter was, as I thought for a while it was yesterday, that it involved a member of the British secret service or the CIA or some such agency that would identify an undercover operative, then I would think so, but it's not in that format anymore. It's a diplomat who's a publicly known person, obviously. So I think identifying that person does not implicate any national security interests that ought to be of concern, as long as that implication remained in private session, so it doesn't become wildly public. And beyond that, I think it's -- I think it's rather clear that the answer should be compelled, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't think you might be better off without it being compelled?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if the Tribunal were to take the position that the evidence will not be considered if he doesn't answer it, then, yeah, I'd prefer that one, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I think the other two matters are matters that initially arose with you. Can you deal first of all with the question of the person who told him to go abroad. Are you satisfied now that we know as much as this witness could possibly tell us about the identity of that person?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I merely said -- I merely noted this is as far as I can go, and then you have to take it from there. This is all I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But it appears from what Mr. Hannis is saying, that the witness has actually given all the information. His direct contact was one of the numbered individuals, and he then mentioned the names of four people who could have been the numbered individual's source and said that he had no more information. Now, do you accept that that is the factual position now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I do not accept that, because he said that number 2 had told him where the order had come from. It is a big order, and here we have Milosevic relaying that through this number 2, who is a low-level operative, sending Tanic to negotiate abroad. We have to understand one thing. Both number 1 and number 2 are defined by Tanic's operatives; that would be the lowest level. In this regard, I want to say that Mr. Hannis asked this morning Witness Tanic whether number 1 and number 2 had had information from any other sources, apart from Mr. Tanic. Number 2 [as interpreted] and number 2 cannot have any information. They are at a very low level. So number 2 cannot send him there. He had to tell him this such and such a person is sending you, and this is who you get the money from. So he merely physically drove him there and physically gave him the money, and Tanic said he knew where the orders had come from. He has to identify the person who had told him that. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. You say that Tanic said he knew where the orders come from. Can you give me the page reference for that, because it's that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that off the cuff. But when I asked him, he said that he didn't want to give us the name of the person because that would bring that person into an unenviable position. After all, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my proposal is not to punish him, but just to simply push this matter aside, and his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these are two separate matters. We can refuse to order him to answer, and then we can make what we can of the evidence, which may or may not be very much. You have to decide whether you are inviting us now to order him to answer the question, identifying that person. We will then have to check the transcript to see if in fact there was a refusal to answer, because it's not clear to me at the moment that there was at the end of the day a refusal to answer. Now, are you saying that there is an order that the Court ought to make on the witness in relation to this issue; and if so, what is the order that you say we should make?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say the same things that Mr. Ackerman said, the same arguments, but I merely allow that there is also the option of you striking off the record the relevant portion of his testimony. I think you should order him to answer this question, pursuant to Rule 70, or punish him because that would be contempt of court. And I would also be satisfied if you were to simply strike off the record the relevant portion of his testimony. So force him to answer; or, if he still refuses to answer, or if you don't want to do it, then simply strike the relevant portions off the record. I think I have been quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Now, on the other matter of the tape and the person who gave access to the tape, what do you have to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this respect, I can say the same thing as I said regarding the first tape. I think that his testimony about this tape has been changed to such an extent and has been to relativised [as interpreted]. And now he doesn't know who it was, whose voice it was, what can be heard. It can be, but it needn't be. I think the most elegant solution would simply be to strike this off the record. But I reiterate all the arguments that I noted in the first instance. I think that Mr. Hannis should simply forget all about these tapes and let them go. And just one more thing. When Mr. Hannis asked about number 1 and number 2, I think that Mr. Tanic did not give the answer to Mr. Hannis's question, but perhaps I'm mistaken here because of interpretation. But it wasn't quite clear when he asked him today, I think that Mr. Hannis would remember. I think it was one of the first questions here. I think that witness was non-responsive, but that's just one remark, and in good-will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When he asked him what, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned colleague asked whether number 1 and number 2 obtained information from other sides, other sources, and I think that the witness did not respond quite clearly to that question. That's what I think. It's page 3, line 11. That's the question that I'm talking about. I think that the answer itself was not quite clear, but this is just a well-meant remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, these submissions -- sorry, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just, one point. If the Chamber is inclined to exclude the evidence, we submit that Rule 95 may be germane in your considerations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I know that yesterday we didn't speak about this, but I think that two remaining persons we have would not reveal the identity. One is the western diplomat, who actually was the only story before the November of this year. The only source for this tape was his western sources or western diplomats regarding the tape. And another one is the official from MUP who gave him the access to the rules of MUP, which were at that time a state secret. So I think that we should consider these two persons as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you didn't ask -- you didn't push the matter at the time when it -- you ought to have addressed it. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to yesterday, Your Honour, but we finished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that -- I don't find that acceptable. We are bending over backwards to accommodate your needs. It's artificial now to try to deal with that issue with the witness. The time to deal with it is in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- when he's faced with it -- no. But to say to him that you're insisting on an answer, and then address us on requiring us to insist on that answer. Now, that didn't happen yesterday, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did insist it with him. I didn't maybe ask that of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly don't have that impression from yesterday's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But at any event, we have the situation where we -- he didn't mention the source, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But if it's just passed over and left to run, there's no reason for the Bench to intervene. The Bench will only intervene where counsel is insisting on an answer, but that he's not getting. We have to be assisted by you in these situations. We've got to know from you what are the answers you insist on getting. Because it's clear in this sort of position, that it could be to your advantage simply to hear from the witness: I'm not telling you. And you make a value judgement that the Bench could never put weight on that and move on; whereas if I insist on getting the person named, it may well be that he'll end up naming him and the Prosecution position will be strengthened. These are value judgements and we rely that you have made the judgement when you push the issue when the witness refuses to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've put us in a difficult position now. One was the person from the MUP who gave him access to the rules, and the other one was?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Western diplomat, who told him about the tape. Only in November of this year, he mentioned the insider from MUP and that he listened to that tape. In previous statements, he was mentioning only this western source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's time for our break. We will return at ten to in closed session and we'll bring the witness in. There are -- there's at least one matter I want to ask him. If there are others that we identify, we can deal with it at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I know you want to break. There is, I believe, still one outstanding issue in relation to this witness and that's his use of his statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm well aware of that and I will deal with that at the end of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have the transcript reference for Mr. Fila's cross-examination in relation to the person who told the witness to go abroad during the war, the part where you say the evidence is now complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Let me find my note. I believe it starts on page 6511, but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which date is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 6511, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm double-checking. I may have transposed digits. It may be --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 6529, line 18, that the question is: "Who told you to go abroad?" That might be what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that deals with the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at 6611, beginning at line 14, Mr. Ackerman is saying: "Who in the SDB authorised you? Is that someone's name you've already given; if so, just say yes." He said: "No, these people were the superiors of those people mentioned in closed session." And if you follow that on down, you'll see where he says it was one of those three or four, but he didn't want to guess. Line 23: "The aforementioned person, the one mentioned in closed session, would be able to tell you who was up the chain of command." At 6612, Mr. Ackerman: "The essence of that big long speech is you don't know who it was, is that true? "A. No, that was not the essence. I cannot give you an answer of which I can be certain." And then he's goes on to explain who they were. He explains: "One cannot leave the country and be given communications equipment and money in wartime without authorisation from high up," et cetera. So it goes on for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- well, first of all, we were discussing what the witness said to me, not to Mr. Ackerman. I have checked the transcript. You have 6509, line 23, I apologise, line 6. 6509, line 6, that's where it begins, and that's where you will find what the witness said in response to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I have to ask you a -- I just actually wanted to be apprised of your -- your political thoughts, because there are a lot of material and materialistic things we have discussed, but we haven't discussed the metaphysical parts. And I think you spoke of many tumultuous events that took place. You also commented that it was a -- there were many misfortunates and about your destiny. And you were accused of material gains. You denied all that. But you did claim that you are a political thinker. Now, I just wanted to know who influenced your thoughts when -- whether you were in adolescence or when you grew up and when you entered all this, because after all you took a career of that sort. And I suggest was it people like Machiavelli, was it people like Chanakya. Was it this great Serb leader Arseniji or anybody else because we would like to understand. And I also suggest that you give us some clue in the same context with respect to the oligarchy with whom you were working in the same context. This is in fact my main question, and this is a brief question which will be later on. I thank you. But I do expect a brief reply, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Initially, the greatest influence was my father. He had been an officer before the war. During the war, he was in a concentration camp, and he was interested in politics. As for the train of thinking, my education rests mainly on Kant and Heideger. Those are my two favorite thinkers, and Huntington in politics. In my political life, my first mentor was Mr. Nebojsa Popov, a well-known intellectual, a socialogist who is well-known in Serbia, and Mrs. Vesna Pesic. That's where I acquired my ideas about liberal democracy and so on. These were the spiritual influences, both remote and direct. I have tried to be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Did you read "The Clash of Civilisation," and do you agree with that, Huntington's book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I see that time has proved them right. They may have been too severe, but conflicts are already arising because of cultural differences, not simply for the same sake of conquering territory. I think he is right to a great extent, although he's not popular among politicians in the west because they feel he is too severe; however, I feel that it is a diagnosis which shows how to avoid a conflict of civilisations. It doesn't mean that it will necessarily come about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And any short comment about the political thinking of the oligarchy and whether the main person you are naming aspired to be like Arseniji.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nebojsa Popov influenced me most. I am happy to be able to repeat his main thesis, which is that the conflicts on the territory of Yugoslavia were a rebellion against modernity. We had a good state, the former Yugoslavia. Of course there were intentions among the republics in that state, but then suddenly people and politicians came to the for, who did not want Yugoslavia to develop further. Because if it developed further, they would not have any place in it anymore. As seen from a sociological and philosophical point of view, it was a large scale of rebellion against modernity. And I could see in that all the republics of the former Yugoslavia, including Serbia. People came to the fore who were simply inventing reasons to pull the republics back, to regress from modernity, even if it required conflicts and crisis. This may be putting it in very blunt terms, but that's the thesis that he held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the last question was had -- they were agreeing -- I mean, the other side was agreeing on anything short of secession. Did that mean a sort of a confrontation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The first chance to save the former Yugoslavia was to transform the Federation into an alliance of sovereign states. That was the first idea held by my party. I did not participate much in its formulation, because I was then a junior politician. But the idea was to transform it into an alliance of sovereign republics, as had been done, for example, in -- well, Russia made an attempt, but the experiment was not successful. In our case, it could have been successful. Each republic could have had full autonomy, be a state within a state, but functioning according to the American system. A joint border, a joint currency, and as such we could have entered the European Union --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I've got your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have had an opportunity during the break to read the parts of the transcript that are required to read to deal with the issue that was outstanding in my mind, so I have no further questions. Mr. Tanic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave, and we'll go into closed session while you leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're now again in open session. The Chamber has decided to make no order obliging the witness to answer. The first matter related to the identity of a NATO diplomat, the Chamber takes the view that the submissions of the Prosecution indicated a potential risk or a risk, in fact, to the national security interests of members of the NATO alliance; and the Prosecutor did not support the application for such an order in the full knowledge that that may result in the Chamber excluding the evidence from consideration or giving it little weight. We can't make a final decision on how to view that evidence until we've heard all the evidence in the case, but the Prosecutor's concern is fully justified. The Chamber will be very circumspect in its approach to that evidence, having taken the view that in the state of its knowledge, it was not prepared to make an order that could compromise the national security interests of a state. In relation to the second point, that was the identity of the person who made the tape available, the witness himself advanced concerns for the security of a member of the security and intelligence services of the Republic of Serbia. The Prosecutor did not positively support the Defence request, although he was at one stage plainly ambivalent about it. In these circumstances, again, the Chamber does not consider it's in a position to conclude that these concerns were not legitimate. In this instance, the risk that the evidence will be excluded completely in due course is even greater than in relation to the first matter. And, again, the Chamber is not in a position to make a final decision on what to do with the evidence, until of course it's heard all the evidence in the case, in case something else comes in that changes the position. So far as the third matter is concerned, that's the instruction to go abroad, we do not consider there is a clear case there of a failure to answer a question. The evidence appears, at the end, to have been as complete an account as the witness was able to give of this. Whether he's telling the truth and whether he's reliability is quite another matter; but on the face of it, it's as complete an account as he could give about the matter. And, therefore, we could not make an order with the obvious consequences of failure to comply with it in these circumstances. In relation to the two matters mentioned by Mr. Lukic, we consider that his interventions came too late for the reasons already discussed; however, we are alert to significant difficulties in relation to the evidence on both matters. And these are matters that can be addressed in submissions at a later stage. So far as the exhibition of the statement of the witness is concerned, then the rule we've -- or the general rule we follow here inevitably means that that whole exhibit is now an exhibit in the case. A number of counsel following Mr. O'Sullivan referred to a large number of paragraphs of the statement without doing as he did, reading the particular paragraphs into the transcript; but their questions clearly assumed that the witness's position was as set out in the statement. And to enable a full understanding of the question asked and the answer given, as necessary -- it will be necessary for the Chamber to consider the statement. But that doesn't carry with it the proposition that we will look at parts of the statement which were not referred to positively by the Prosecution and take them as evidence, positive evidence, for the Prosecution case; we will take the statement in the context - that's the parts not directly admitted in the Prosecution case - we will take in the context of the questions and the answers given when various passages were being referred to. Now, because of that, Mr. O'Sullivan, it is necessary for the Defence to produce a properly redacted version of this, which would become the public version in the case. Meanwhile, all parts after paragraph - someone will need to remind me of the paragraph, the final paragraph admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All paragraphs after 45 will be admitted under seal until that is done. It may be, Mr. O'Sullivan, you should be passing the buck to someone else in the circumstances, but someone has to take responsibility and the matter mustn't remain outstanding. So could we have it done by Tuesday at the latest, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That deals with all outstanding matters arising from the evidence of that witness. Your next witness, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness will be Richard Ciaglinski. There is one matter with the last witness, Your Honour, the excerpt of the book, "The Road to Rambouillet," now does have an exhibit number; it's P2511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a matter with the last witness I neglected to mention earlier. During my cross-examination, I mentioned the eight-day OTP statement of General Perisic, and you inquired if he had ever been asked about Operation Horseshoe. I've searched those with a word search programme, computer word search programme. The word "horseshoe" doesn't seem to have appeared either as a question or an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may not be the complete answer; I don't fault you for that. It may have been asked in a different way. I was concerned to know what the value of reference to Perisic's statement was, unless we knew that the issue had in some way or another been explored or unless we knew that questions had been asked that you would have expected to elicit the answer that this -- a reference to this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my colleagues might correct me. But my recollection, as I stand here right now, is that those interviews took place after the testimony in Milosevic that we were talking about. And Mr. Nice, who was a Prosecutor in Milosevic, was a questioner in those -- in those interviews. And so one would expect if he had any credence in the Operation Horseshoe testimony of this witness, that he certainly would have asked it of Perisic. But that's very nebulous, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the form placed in front of you..

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning. First off, I've been reminded by the court reporter and the translators that since you and I both speak the same language, that we need to pause between the end of my question and your answer, and me after your answer before my next question. Could you please tell us your name and spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right. My name is Richard Ciaglinski, spelled C-i-a-g-l-i-n-s-k-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And may I call you Colonel Ciaglinski or Mr. Ciaglinski? Do you have a preference?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I don't mind at all, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, you were a, as I understand it, a career soldier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: About two and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to give a statement to ICTY investigators in March of the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, more recently, did you give a short supplementary statement to other representatives of the ICTY on the 1st of November of this year?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this -- those two have been put together as one document, which bears exhibit number P2488. This witness is being offered under Rule 92 ter for both his statement and his transcript. I will first go through a few questions about some minor corrections in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel Ciaglinski, on Tuesday of this week, did you have occasion to meet with Ms. Carter and myself to go through your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of doing that, did you note a couple of things that we needed to correct and bring to the Court's attention?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, on page 2 of his 2000 statement, in the middle of the page, there's a reference to: "In October of 1988."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: About your being based at the headquarters of the UK support command. Was that 1988 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It was 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe on page 8, in the next-to-last paragraph, we noted that General Lazarevic's name was misspelled by one letter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Finally, on page 10 of your 2000 statement. We'll address this in more detail in a moment, but you indicated that you had photographs of this pile of burning documents and would make those available to the ICTY. Except for one photo, which is now marked P2504, were you able to locate the photos you had taken of that burning pile of documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: What happened was that a lot of time has elapsed since the -- Mr. Milosevic's trial, and we also moved house several times. And my wife, being an extremely good housekeeper, she threw away a lot of stuff, and I think she might have gone through my photographs and paperwork and threw it out. So the only picture I had left was the one I submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was the one you were able to provide us was the one or the best one you had in mind when you described that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Not at all. Unfortunately, it's one taken from an angle that doesn't actually show it very well at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with your statement, having noted those corrections, are you otherwise satisfied having reviewed your statements and can you attest that that March 2000 statement and your November 2006 statement are true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief; and if you were asked the same questions, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Exhibit P2489, Your Honours, the transcripts of Colonel Ciaglinski from his testimony in the Milosevic case in April of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have a chance to review your transcripts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And having done so, are you satisfied that they accurately reflect what your evidence was in that case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say, "in general," you have a reservation about whether they're accurate or --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, a lot of time has elapsed and memory plays tricks on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Was there anything you noted that you thought was a mistake in how your evidence was taken down?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and remembrance and belief at this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. It's just surprising when you read back through it, how much was said and done, and I would say it's difficult to remember everything that happened four or five years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you attest that you would give the same answers today if asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. If you don't, I'm sure it will be brought to your attention by one or more of us in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that, I would tender his transcripts of Exhibit 2489.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, your written evidence in the form of the transcript and your statements is in evidence. The Judges have read it. If -- or if not, they will read it. So I will try not to repeat needlessly everything that is down, but I do want to highlight a few things. Can you tell us briefly, you began your military career in 1974?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in late 1998, you volunteered for and were accepted as a member of the OSCE's Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date you started your duties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I flew out to Macedonia, and I think I was in Kosovo around the -- the end of the first week of December, somewhere around the 5th, 6th, 7th; and I believe I started my duties in Pristina around the 9th, 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you based in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I was based in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you travel throughout Kosovo during the -- during your tenure there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was your primary role or duties during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Initially, the OSCE intended me to run the -- be one of the major instructors of the training centre at Brezovica; but I was taken to Pristina, as it was felt I had other skills which might be valuable. And I understudied Donna Phelan, who was in charge of weapons and arms verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then subsequently, what was your main job during the rest of your stay in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: When Donna Phelan's job was -- when she moved to run the fusion centre for a time, I was then moved across to -- being in charge of weapons and verification. And I also then took on the responsibilities of liaison with both the Serbian side and the KLA, but the KLA -- the two duties were incompatible. So I just focussed on the Serbian commission for cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A few follow-up questions on that answer. First of all, you mentioned the fusion centre. Can you explain briefly what that was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously, we had a lot of people in the field who sent in information of what they saw, people they spoke to. They would write reports and send it back to Pristina, to our headquarters, where the information would be collated and fused together to make a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, initially, you say you took on the responsibilities of liaison with both the Serb side and the KLA, but these duties were incompatible. Can you tell us briefly how you came to that determination?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The -- certainly my impression and others around me was that it was very difficult to work with both side and have both sides trust you; and therefore, either side could suspect me of passing information to the other side. And I also felt personally, and I think my bosses felt, that it was for the sake of myself and for my credibility, to just focus on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you indicated that you became the liaison for the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was your immediate supervisor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: My immediate boss at all times was General DZ, Drewienkiewcz.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And DZ is an abbreviation or a nickname, because his full last name is somewhat difficult to spell and pronounce?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout his career in the British military, he was referred to as DZ, because it has all the letters of the alphabet from D to Z.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mention in your statement, in the English page 2, the last paragraph, I'm sorry, I don't have the B/C/S in front of me, that in relation to VJ site visits that you were doing, there were three main VJ sites that you wanted to visit. Do you recall where those were or what those were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. They were three company group locations that we were allowed to visit on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the geographic location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, there was -- there was one in the south overlooking the main road that went to the Prizren. There was one up in the north and one in the central, sort of western district.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned this Commission on Cooperation. First of all, can you tell us what that was.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It was an organisation in Pristina located in the administration building where the administration of Kosovo was situated, and it was one of several. There was another higher-level contact point, obviously in Belgrade, where General Bo Pelmas was working. There was one in Pristina normally composed of General Loncar, who was in charge; Colonel Kotur; Colonel Mijatovic; various people over the time from the Foreign Ministry and Interior Ministry, as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General Loncar and Colonel Kotur were members of what body or agency?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This cooperation commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And outside the cooperation commission, what were they? Were they police, military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. Colonel Kotur was a retired -- was a Serbian military officer, I understand, in the intelligence services; and General Loncar was a retired general who had a long successful career, well-respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Colonel Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: He was the deputy to General Lukic, working with the MUP in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And representatives on your side, on KVM, was it just you or?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, in theory, the representation should have been at the very highest level. So the meetings were designed, I suppose, for the ambassadors or director Walker to attend, which he delegated to General DZ who attended very many of the meetings. But the meetings General DZ couldn't attend, I was delegated to represent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And over time, did it transpire that you became the primary attendee on behalf of KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I probably attended 90 percent of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How often did the commission meet?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Once a day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Usually once a day, sometimes two or three times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you weren't attending meetings of the cooperation commission, what were you doing to carry out your duties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I would be usually in the field. General DZ would use me as a person who would travel around and solve problems for him in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess I should back up for a minute. I jumped ahead of what our evidence has been in this case so far. Can you tell us how the KVM came to be created, and what its primary job was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Certainly. It was the result of following UN resolutions, and it -- the document, which actually created and gave the terms of reference of the KVM, was the meeting of the document signed by Mr. Geremek, I believe, on the 16th of October, 1998. And in that document, it quite specifically details what our composition and what our duties and rights were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit P658, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of the details of this agreement? Did you have a copy of it that you referred to while carrying out your duties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I carried a copy at all times. In fact, there were three documents, and I would carry usually all three somewhere in one of my pockets, just in case I was ever challenged or questioned about access or what our duties were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did that ever happen during course of carrying out your duties that you got challenged about your right to be where you were or doing what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, often.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm waiting for a moment here to see if we can show you one of those documents. That one that you referred to is as the Geremek agreement is one of the three. Do you recall what the other two were that you had or who would sign them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. There was one signed by Nauman and the other one was signed by Shaun Burns. So only on one of the three documents, there were signatures. I believe Mr. Sainovic, Milosevic, Clark Nauman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we seem to be having some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document that's on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And which one of the three is that that we've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is the main Geremek agreement. He was the chairman in office of the OSCE at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you rely on one of the provisions of that agreement as your authority to go basically anywhere in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It comes under the terms of reference, and it guarantees our ability to move and access anywhere in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page of both the English and the B/C/S, please. Could we go to the top of the page -- the very top of the page. I'm sorry, Your Honour. May I have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think we have to go one more page, I believe. Yes, at the very bottom of that first page and then on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you read item number 1 and then we'll turn the next page for you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: "The verification mission will travel throughout Kosovo to verify ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then can we go to the next page to the very top.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please continue if you have it on the left.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: "The maintenance of the cease-fire by all elements. It will investigate reports of cease-fire violations. Mission personnel will have full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in real life on the ground, did it work out that way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly how it did work or not work.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I suppose initially our freedom of movement was greater; but as time went along and more and more military operations and police operations being carried out, we were prevented from entering many areas. There were two really main sort of things we were interested in. One was verifying what was happening on the ground, but we were also interested in verifying what was happening and what was going on and being stored inside military barracks and installations and garrisons. So in regard to the -- the barracks, we did try to carry out on-the-spot, no-notice inspections, but that met with zero -- well, zero possibility. We were not allowed to carry out inspection. We were held outside barracks, not allowed in; and in fact threatened if we -- told if we didn't remove our vehicles as well as ourselves, it would cause an incident of some sort of some severity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did you bring this up with when you had access denied? Was that something discussed at the cooperation commission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
