utterances.text: Yes. Obviously our point of contact for all these matters was the cooperation commission. When the incident was happening, we would obviously report it to the people on the ground denying us access, saying we would have to go back to Pristina, to the cooperation commission, and to General Loncar, and to voice our protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to trying to carry out the on-site inspections, were you also trying to verify when there were reports of conflict or violations of the cease-fire by either side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, in accord with the agreement, that was one of our major tasks; and we would try to establish who the guilty parties were, what would cause the problems, and the extent of damage or injury. If we didn't have access, then obviously we couldn't do our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement of March 23rd, 2000, at the bottom of page 3, the last paragraph, you state that it was your view that Loncar and his subordinates really saw the Commission of Cooperation and the KVM as a means of proving to the world that they were the innocent party, but they were very specific as to what they wanted us to verify. It goes on to the next page: "Whenever something happened to a Serb force, they would call us up and ask us to come down and verify the event, but they would not allow us to verify events that they had caused." First of all, how do you know about that, that they wouldn't wanton allow you to verify events that they had caused? What was your source of information about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, it was the verifiers on the ground and of myself in person. If an incident took place, you know, we would send out personnel from the local field office or the local regional centre or from Pristina to try and investigate what was going on. And these people would then go there, try to do their work. If they couldn't or if they could, regardless, they would write a report as to what happened. And they would state that they did have difficulty, if they did have difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the moment off the top of your head, can you give the Court an example where you or your verifiers were not allowed to verify something that you believed or had information that the Serbs had caused in terms of a violation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: There were quite a few incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were those reported? Did you have a daily or a monthly report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. We had a daily reporting system, and we also kept all the documents in the blue book. They were compiled regularly, daily, in the blue book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many branch offices did you have?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: We had five regional centres throughout the whole of Kosovo; and then we would have houses in various villages, field offices, a great many of those. We were very well spread in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many verifiers in total did you have in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I believe by the end, we had 1.400 or there about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With relation to the cooperation commission, you say in your statement, page 4, at the beginning of the page that General Loncar initially appeared to be the representative of the Federal Government, but over time it appeared that his authority diminished.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In what way did you notice that his authority appeared to diminish over time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, initially our dealings with General Loncar and the commission, we would get answers very quickly to our questions. And General Loncar was present at all the meetings. And as the time progressed, then General Loncar would appear less and less frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the that time, you say he regularly went back to Belgrade. How often did he go?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, towards -- and maybe in February/March, March especially, he was there, I would say, almost every week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement page 4, paragraph 2, you describe an incident around Christmas of 1998, I believe the 27th of December, 1998, where you had a meeting with General Loncar and he told you about the Albanians having captured a Serb farmer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us why that was significant and what happened. Where did that take place, first of all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right. The incident -- the way we learned about it in the first place was at the end of almost a three-hour meeting. We were informed by General Loncar that we should be aware that they had -- the Serbian authorities had decided to launch an action the south-west of Podujevo, on what we or referred to as an area sort of a tank hill, but really was towards the villages of Gornja Lapastica and Obrandza. It came as a surprise because although we knew that the Serbian army -- the VJ army had been deployed south-east of Podujevo - which again came as a surprise because the units were not really supposed to be deployed from the barracks, but we were assured that this was a recognised training area. And one of the agreements does allow for the VJ to carry out normal training. But we knew where these -- the tanks were, the T-55 tanks, and also the artillery were located on this old, disused air-field. And it didn't seem a great problem because they weren't actually doing very much. But then when General Loncar announced that this unit would be one of the units taking part in this action to free what appeared to be a farmer that the KLA had captured, it -- and also knowing what I knew, that what was waiting on the other side of the mountain, around Obrandza, I knew that this could actually escalate into quite a vicious battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you know what was waiting on the other side of the mountains?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we visited -- Podujevo was one of the hot spots for problems. The KLA had a habit of using snipers to shoot -- shoot up military VJ convoys coming to resupply the garrisons in Kosovo. And so we were very often up there talking to the unit on the hill overlooking the area, which had replaced the KLA. And it was also the -- not far from the headquarters or the Remi, one of the KLA commanders who were very active in that area; and, therefore, I had spent almost part of every day in that area. So I was aware what was happening from the other side. So the KLA were preparing a defence by bringing in additional forces and equipment, ammunition. It was no secret. I believe the other side could have seen it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Podujevo is located in the north of --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's just north of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Along the main -- one of the main north-south roads between Kosovo and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I would say that the road passing by to the east of Podujevo was the main re-supply route and the main communication route to Serbia, Belgrade, Nis, and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this seems to be a large engagement of forces on both sides involving the kidnapping or holding of one Serbian civilian.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, what had happened earlier is that the -- a unit of the MUP had attempted to rescue this farmer and had come under heavy fire and sustained a number of injuries, serious injuries. And therefore, it was believed by the VJ and the MUP, I presume, that a stronger, larger, force would be necessary to take out this one farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Including tanks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yeah. It's unusual to use regiment or two regiments of tanks and artillery, but it probably would work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Knowing what you knew about the KLA forces on the other side and the proposed contingent for the Serbian force, you told us you had some concerns about what might happen. What did you do to try and prevent that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we were always being accused or goaded by the commission that the OSCE did nothing. We just reported in a biased way; and that we, you know, didn't get our hands dirty, basically, by doing anything. And I saw an opportunity here to actually show that we -- that we might try to do something, which would actually defuse the situation, by volunteering to actually go and talk to the KLA and ask the KLA to release the farmer; and, thereby, preventing what we believed to have been a major escalation of the violence and a great number of lives being lost on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you volunteered yourself or proposed to do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did. And I suggested that myself, David Wilson, my colleague who had relations with the KLA, and maybe a member of the Red Cross should go in and attempt this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what did -- you described some of it in your statement. General Loncar heard this proposal from you and thought it was a good idea?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I think he was quite surprised. I was quite surprised myself that I offered; but, yes, he said that it was an interesting proposal. But he wasn't able to actually make a decision as to whether we could actually do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what did he do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: He suggested that he went out and made a phone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learn who he called?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. My first guess was that he was going to call Mr. Sainovic, because we knew that Mr. Sainovic had a prominent role. He was responsible for Kosovo, deputy prime minister; therefore, he probably could or would know who to get authority from to carry this action out. I subsequently discovered, by talking to members of the commission, when I suggested that it was Mr. Sainovic; they said, "No. It was even higher than Mr. Sainovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge of who was in the hierarchy, who was higher than Mr. Sainovic with regard to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, when I was told that, you know, you can't imagine how high -- in what a high position the person was. I could only imagine at the time that it was Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then you had the approval, and you went and tried to resolve this matter by getting the farmer out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I first of all while the phone calls were taking place, I was on the phone to my headquarters giving the -- passing the proposal to them for their approval, because there was always the chance that they might say no. And while I was doing this, the approval came through that -- in fact, that the action would be held at bay to give us a chance to carry out the rescue of the farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you succeed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It took most of the day, but we managed to get the farmer out and hand him over to the police of Podujevo, police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: And there was no subsequent action following that by the forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 615, please, this is a Kosovo atlas at page 19, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When the map comes up, Colonel, I would ask if you could locate on there the location where this occurred. Did you get anyone else out besides the farmer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: We managed to take out as part of the sort of deal, we managed to get a wounded Albanian out as well. Nothing is simple in this world. There is always a quid pro quo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Kosovo Albanians wouldn't let you take the farmer out unless you took out their wounded comrade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you take him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: He was taken to a clinic in Pristina, where he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the area that's depicted on the map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we Pristina on the lower left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we enlarge the upper left corner. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, do you know where Podujevo would be on this map --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Podujevo is at the very top, this side of the -- top left-hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where we see a little bit of orange and the railroad track --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, the railroad track -- in fact, we're now getting to the Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We see it better now. Can you indicate the area where this occurred.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb VJ forces were based on this air-field here shown in yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: And I did, in fact, spend several days sitting just outside their position following the incident -- well, before and following the incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, since you were here before, technology has moved on. The pointer you've got there doesn't work with the equipment we now have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's wonderful. Oh, there's a pointer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this time things have to be marked on the screen for us to be able to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis will probably ask you to mark something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With that pen you can actually draw on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could draw us a circle around the air-field.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, the air-field is there, and the forces are basically dug-in inside that air-field complex. It was a disused air-field, and I spent several days sort of sitting on a road in this area where.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where you've made an X inside the circle.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The X was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you indicate where the KLA positions were.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the Obradza, so we are talking about an area, as indicated now by that very untidy circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've made a large circle to the west of Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was the Serbian contingent with the tanks that was proposed to be used to rescue this farmer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Can the map be raised a bit or dropped a bit more, so we can see more of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think. On this map, we are at the top.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Exactly. I can't remember. But -- looking at the main road, somewhere in this area here, I believe, was the tank position, tank hill. And then the village where the Serb was being kept was back in this area here, in Lapastica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we take a screen shot of that and give it the next in-court number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC109, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think I need the pen anymore on that, Colonel. I want to ask you then about some subsequent meetings. You mentioned a meeting that took place on the 6th of January, 1999, at the government building in Pristina at page 5 of your statement, third paragraph -- or fourth paragraph from the top. This was in the conference room of Mr. Andjelkovic, who was the Serb administrator.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was this a usual meeting of the cooperation commission, or was this some kind of unusual extraordinary meeting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I think it -- well, I think it was an extraordinary meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how so? Why was it out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, there were several major issues which had been resolved to our satisfaction and making our life extremely difficult, making the KVM's duty duties very difficult and in some cases impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: There was a whole list of issues that were dealt with. The meeting was chaired by Mr. Sainovic. And, for example, our rescue helicopter which we had sitting outside of Kosovo, which we had arranged to cas-evac any casualties that we had and which was on the entrance and exit of Kosovo, was covered by the Geremek agreement; and permission had never been given for us to bring the helicopter in. We had problems with lack of fuel. We found it very difficult to get diesel fuel for our Land Rovers. Most fuel stations refused to sell it to us. There was also the issue of the KLA prisoners who were being kept in a prison in Nis, and access to those prisoners. And of course, there's always the issue of fair or unfair verification. Mr. Sainovic did in fact give us quite a hard time in accusing us of not verifying fairly and just reporting really the misdemeanours of the Serbian side, never mentioning the KLA side and the Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the next paragraph of your statement you mention that some of the attendees at this meeting included Ambassador Keller. Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Ambassador Keller was one of the deputies to Ambassador Walker and he was probably our -- the main contact with Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, General Maisonneuve. He was representing General DZ. He was in charge of one of the regional centres. When General DZ was away, he was standing in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who chaired the meeting? Who ran the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The meeting was run completely by Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to page 6 of your statement and at page 6, paragraph 4, you mention Colonel Kotur. What was his role on the commission? Was he subordinate to General Loncar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was subordinate to General Loncar, and he was -- he had the contact -- he was the point of contact of the commission with the VJ units in Kosovo. He certainly was able to -- if ever we had any problems with the -- of access or questions to be asked or visits, then Colonel Kotur would facilitate those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the nature of your relationship with him, given your role as an OSCE/KVM representative to the commission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I think on the personal side, we got on quite well; and we sort of spent a lot of time together sort of visiting units, working on the border. Every day I could -- I would be with him for three or four hours at these meetings of the cooperation commission; and, therefore, we were -- I wouldn't say we were close, but we actually sort of knew each other quite well, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your statement page 7, paragraph 1, you indicate that sometime during the last weeks that Colonel Kotur was there, he told you about a proposed manoeuvre plan that was going to be used for an operation to eliminate the KLA. Can you tell us how that came about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. It was right towards the end when we'd already decided, I believe, to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when would that have been, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, the -- you mean the decision to leave or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or the leaving.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, the leave -- the decision to leave and the planning to leave was -- you can take that right back to somewhere shortly after Christmas, when Ambassador Walker ordered us to make plans for a possible evacuation at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then when did you actually leave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: We didn't leave until the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in that time-frame, between Christmas and your leaving in -- near the end of March, when was this --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. This discussion with Colonel Kotur, which came as a surprise to me, happened a few days before we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was present when this discussion took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, it was -- it was following one of our sort of final meetings at which the commission had been present; and when everybody else had gone, I was -- I remained with my interpreter and Colonel Kotur was sort of seeing us out of the building or was going to see us out of the building. But prior to that, he suddenly took me to a map on the table and told me something unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it just the two of you, or was anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No, there was just Colonel Kotur, myself, and the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what language was the conversation being carried out in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Kotur spoke in Serbian. I don't think he -- I'm sure he didn't speak English. He might have understood some English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you speak or understand any Serbian?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But did the interpreter interpret for both of you, or just for him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: For both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened? What was unusual in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, during -- during our entire time there and my relationship with Colonel Kotur, you know, we spent a lot of time in the field and dangerous situations and, you know, I would call a spade a spade if I regarded something as a terrorist incident carried out by terrorists, I would call it that way. And I think we built up a respect as colleagues, as professionals. And he suddenly just turned to me and said, I will show you how we will deal with the KLA and with the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did he say when this was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: After our departure. He said that -- this was something they would have to do, because it would save NATO a job in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he specify what he meant by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. But I am -- my interpretation was that there was a problem with -- a Muslim problem or a Kosovar problem that if they've dealt with it, then we wouldn't have to deal with it in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did he then proceed to detail you about how this was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, with his hand he actually pointed out on the map how he -- what he thought was actually going to happen and how the military action would take place to displace the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I show you a map that you've used before in connection with that, will that assist you in recalling how he said it was going to go?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit Number 2484, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your recollection is that he mentioned both the KLA and the --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- population, meaning the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. He -- I will not paraphrase exactly how it was, but the gist was they would deal -- get rid of the KLA, and they would remove the Albanians from Kosovo forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know, is that too small or --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you deal with that again. This is a map of Kosovo, and there are some green lines. Can you explain to the Judges what this is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is a green line I drew on this map during the trial of Mr. Milosevic. If I had a pointer, I could point maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you want to use the pen to mark on the screen, or do you want to point --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I can describe. I can describe. The activity was due to start in the top right-hand corner where it says "Serbia," but the activity was actually going to take place in the Vucitrn area and the Glogovac. And he basically just showed me the directions that he thought -- well, he said the military would be moving to push and then cut off and kill groups of KLA. So first of all, in the area of Vucitrn, towards Glogovac, Mitrovica; and then also have forces push across from Podujevo across the mountains through Remi sort of territory, push the KLA into areas where they would be dealt with as well. So it's far more complex, the actual -- obviously, the logistics of this and the planning of this. But in general the activity would take place up there, and then it would sort of move down. As you can see southwards, across to Prizren, up to Djakovica, Decani, and ending in Pec. And on the way, sort of, mopping up those pockets of KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That describes what the plan was with regard to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he say anything about what would happen with the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. I was just told that they would be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in your answer before the most recent one Remi's area. Who was he and what was his area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The area between, if you like, to the west of Podujevo, but not quite as far as Mitrovica-Vucitrn, because then you're crossing areas -- other areas where people I think like Rahman was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell me who Remi and Rahman were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, Remi was the local KLA commander in the Podujevo area, a very dangerous man. He didn't say very much. I think his actions spoke for his words. Rahman was another commander, local commander, who was probably even more dangerous. And my only dealings with Remi, I attended several meetings in his headquarters as an observer very early on. With Rahman, later on I was dealing with trying to get the release of captured VJ soldiers who'd accidentally driven into his area, into Rahman's area, and were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Colonel Kotur tell you why he was telling you this? It seems an unusual thing for him to do.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, in the sort of few meetings preceding this, he was basically -- he told me he was fed up with all the politicking. He was fed up with the whole situation. It wasn't really getting anywhere, and it was time for some action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he still on the cooperation commission at this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It was very strange because I was told at an earlier meeting, when we had been -- General Loncar announced that we were getting a new commission headed up by General Brankovic, and I was told then that Kotur's position would be replaced by Colonel Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that happened? How long before you left?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Oh, a few weeks. Not that long, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any other conversations with Colonel Kotur after this date when he showed you this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- move on to that, if I may. Your statement doesn't appear to me to refer to civilians at all as part of this, unless I'm missing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it says -- does it say "Albanians?" I can't remember. I'm sure I mentioned both in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's not a reference in the written statement, but I believe there's a reference in his prior testimony in Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, in Milosevic, yes. In your statement, you actually say: "It appeared to me that Kotur had become totally disillusioned," which you've just been saying "by the whole thing and the pending departure of the OSCE. And there was only one remaining option to eliminate the KLA." Now, is that a legitimate military objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the KLA, by this time, had actually become a -- a military -- fairly substantial military force of possibly 10.000 armed personnel. So I suppose if they were waging war on the VJ and the police force, on the country, on the people, then I would say it probably was a legitimate target, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You testified in the Milosevic case about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that time, you mentioned this conversation with Colonel Kotur in private session, I believe.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because at the time you had a concern for his safety?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Colonel Kotur well, and I also had met his wife, who was an interpreter and an assistant to the secretary of Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you consider yourselves friends as well as working colleagues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we spent several sort of evenings in Kosovo in military units, where we sort of ate and drank together, and we did tour extensively around Kosovo together. So I think we were colleagues. I wouldn't say that we were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You're aware that Colonel Kotur testified in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I read the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you aware of what he said about this conversation that you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. He denied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement of November of this year, you talk about this. Did you have any contact from Colonel Kotur and/or his wife after your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I had two contacts with the Kotur family. One was shortly after I left the area in June of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was that about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I had returned to my job in Rhinedahalen in the headquarters, and Mrs. Kotur rang me to ask if I could help her regain their apartment from Pristina, which had been taken from them and handed over to some Albanian families. And indeed I tried to use my contacts to try and facilitate this, unsuccessfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the only subject that you talked about on that occasion in June 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We exchanged -- she faxed me documents and title deeds, which I then passed back to the UN headquarters in Pristina, but that was the main topic of conversation. Several phone calls and several passages of faxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But all about that subject?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next time you had contact from either Mrs. Kotur or Colonel Kotur would have been when?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This was post the -- my giving evidence at the Milosevic trial, and I was working in the British embassy in Sopija as the Defence attache. I received a phone call from the switchboard to tell me that there is a lady from Kosovo is on the phone. So I spoke to her, not realising it was Mrs. Kotur.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And she's an interpreter. She speaks English?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: She speaks excellent English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your conversation was in English?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was this about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This was a rather bizarre call because initially she sort of launched a tirade against me for destroying her husband's reputation, career, prospects, the possibility of remaining in decent military housing, their relationship with their friends as a result of my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At that time had your testimony been made public, or was it still under seal, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I know that -- well, I hope that the name of Colonel Kotur had been kept out of any documents or transcripts which had been published on the ICTY web site.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ask her how she'd become aware that you had mentioned --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No, I was -- you can imagine how I felt when I'd suddenly been accused of destroying everything that the Koturs had ever cherished or had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, my response was silence, at which point she said to me, "But I forgive you. Come and have lunch with us at Nis."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I passed -- I ran this information past my ambassador, past other people in the embassy, and they all advised me that it probably was unwise for me to go to Serbia to have lunch with the Koturs, bearing in mind that during the -- following my testimony, there was quite bad reaction, I believe, to me and my evidence. And the -- my colleague, the defence attach in Belgrade had actually warned me off at that time shortly after the evidence not to go to Belgrade for my own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say a bad reaction to you and your evidence, bad reaction on the part of whom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I -- I believe that there was some threat to me and my personal well-being from people who believed I'd lied or sort of besmirched the name of the VJ or the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And any other conversations with Mrs. Kotur or Colonel Kotur since that day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No, not at all. I said I would get back to her and I did not. I did actually pass the information to the -- my colleague at the Serbian embassy, and also I raised the matter with his ambassador, the ambassador of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is that a suitable time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's a good time, Your Honour, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to have a break now, Mr. Ciaglinski, for half an hour or so. Would you please just leave with the courtroom with the usher, who will show you where to wait.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, in the direct evidence in Milosevic, where does this actually arise? Can you give me a page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It appears -- I'm having trouble reading the small print. It looks like it's on page 3224, lines 5 through 7, and it looks like it was on the 14th of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask counsel and witness to make pauses between question and answer if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, we just talked about the contact with Mrs. Kotur. One other item in your statement of 2006 I wanted to ask you again concerning -- I have to go back to the Podujevo incident around Christmas of 1998. In your statement you say at page 2 of the 2006 statement at the bottom, that in a meeting with Loncar and others you were told that this deployment by the Serb forces was allowed under the October agreements because it was a training ground. Did you have some considerations about where the training areas where in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The -- it was a -- it became an issue as more and more units started to deploy outside the garrison and barrack areas, and so we raised the question: What constituted a training area? And some areas, like the air-field south-east of Podujevo had actually been used for a number of years as a deployment area during exercises. But the answer which surprised all of us was when we were told that basically the whole of Kosovo was a training area and it could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Every -- every square metre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That's what we were told. It was that Kosovo had been used or traditionally was -- had been, would be a training area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did that impact your ability to carry out your job of verification?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, the problem was that it was difficult enough with the verifiers we had to keep tabs on all the activities going on; but once the units deployed into the field it made our job, I would say, say nigh on impossible, mainly because once the units deployed in the field, they would close off all the areas, so all the access tracks, roads, routes would be sealed. So the areas could be 10 by 10 kilometres or 20 by 20 kilometres. So if there was any activity happening in those areas, we just had no way of getting in and verifying anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did those training areas that were established sometimes include villages where civilians were living?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, the -- as I said, the training areas that we were told about and we observed did include villages because it was difficult not to include villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to what you said earlier about there came a time where General Loncar and Colonel Kotur were replaced on the Commission For Cooperation. You indicated -- in your statement, you say that they were replaced by General Ilija Brankovic, who replaced Loncar, and Colonel Petrovic replaced Colonel Kotur. Was there a change in the relationship between you, the OSCE/KVM on one hand and the Serbs with this new contingent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, there was. From what had been a working relationship that we could make work and where we could get difficult points across or even sort of have fast reaction for certain activities, we went from that to a position where the whole thing just slowed down. General Brankovic announced that in future the meetings would have to be announced ahead. The points for the agenda would have to be submitted 24 hours in advance, which therefore meant we couldn't deal with anything current. And in Kosovo things were happening by the minute. There was no way of guessing what was going to happen in 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he insist on that condition for the duration of your time there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: He tried to be insistent and our reaction was that we wouldn't comply with that -- with these new specifications. And I think we tried it once or twice, and eventually we were allowed to sort of go back to our 10.00 type meeting. But it was difficult. It was nowhere near as useful or cooperative as the mission had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me change gears on you now and go forward -- well, perhaps not forward depending on what date the change took place. In paragraph -- on page 8, paragraph 4 of your statement, you mentioned the events in Racak on the 15th of January, 1999. And you say you later learned that NATO had intercepted radio traffic that showed the Serbs were more heavily involved in this massacre than they were admitting, and they gave orders to actually kill people. Who was your source for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just on the Racak matter, we have Your Honour's order concerning Racak and I'm not sure if Mr. Hannis's question is in the spirit of that order when he talks about he's now trying to assess responsibility for what happened there. And I think that that does not comport with the -- both the letter and the spirit of Your Honour's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question he's actually asked is for an identification of the source for the information. So there's no breach of any earlier order in that, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, what concerned me, Your Honour, was the statement that showed that the Serbs were more heavily involved in this massacre than they were admitting. I think that gets right into the merits of the case, Your Honour. It is very difficult for us to rebut that under the letter and the spirit of Your Honour's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness hasn't given an answer that would give rise to that problem, Mr. Sepenuk, and the question he's been asked is a much more specific one. So as and when the problem arises, we shall address it. But meanwhile that question can be answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're being asked, Mr. Ciaglinski, for your source for that information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, both sides by this point were monitoring each of the telephone and radio traffic. And when I went -- when we left Kosovo, I was the liaison officer between the OSCE and the NATO headquarters, General Jackson. And I had to occasionally be in the intelligence cell of that headquarters. And this was certainly something which was discussed, radio-telephone traffic monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You just -- your answer said radio-telephone monitoring. In your statement you say "radio." Do you recall what you knew at the time or what you were told about where this information came from? Was it intercepted telephone conversations or radio communications or both?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I wasn't able to ascertain whether it was telephone or radio, but it was communications. We have communications centres that cover both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to page 9 of your statement, and it's the fourth paragraph on that page. You describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The -- I take it, Mr. Hannis, that the part there -- I've rather, I think, been unfair in what I've said to Mr. Sepenuk because I was ignoring or overlooking the fact that there is a statement here in front of us. It's not simply a question and an answer that we are dealing with. Now, the question of orders may be relevant if in some way there is implication of the accused here. The Chamber is interested in evidence which shows the relationship between the activity that might be characterised as a crime and the conduct or exercise of responsibilities of the accused. We are not interested, as you know, about the details of the events in Racak in this trial. Now, can I take it that that answer there is to remain -- or that statement is to remain in the very unspecific form in which we see it at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've talked about the difficulty in completely not speaking the word "Racak," because I think that's nearly impossible to do. But this evidence is offered for a couple of other purposes, too, rather than showing whether or not there was a killing and massacre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not preventing you asking these questions. I just wanted to know if anything was -- anything more was going to be explored about what these -- or who was involved in giving these orders that might be of relevance to the case against the accused here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had testimony from the previous witness about phone conversations between two of the accused concerning these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a newspaper article about that. What I'm trying to show -- and our witness said that some of his sources for that information came from western sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm trying to connect things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Now the Chamber will not prevent you from exploring this issue to do that, but I can also re-assure Mr. Sepenuk that we will be giving no weight to the specific allegation about what happened in Racak. That's there simply to give context to what might otherwise be relevant information about the chain of responsibility. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, on page 9 of your statement, the fourth paragraph down, you describe an incident that you saw along the Podujevo-Pristina road where a VJ colonel was shot, and then there was an operation carried out by the VJ to try and deal with that sniper. You've described that that appeared to be carried out in a professional manner, that there wasn't any wholesale shelling or attack on the village, no destruction, no killings, no retribution. You were there watching when this happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I had been in Podujevo, and I was on my way back when I came across the blockage of the road next to this village. I can't remember, the name was Lebane, Lebana. And I was intrigued about what was happening. There was no police involved at all. There was an army, VJ, operation and I was allowed to travel up and down the road, go and look at some of the military units that were involved, and I was able to see the entire operation from the west side of the road through my binoculars standing next to a VJ T-55 tank. And I saw nothing improper at all. It was a well-conducted military quarterman's search of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you there in your KVM vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How was it marked to distinguish it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: My -- our vehicles were bright orange. This was something that was decided earlier on in the mission because UN vehicles tend to be white, but there was a problem with some of the Serbian police vehicles also being white. And to avoid any confusion and to make our vehicles stand out, General DZ I think decided to have them painted in an outrageous colour, which seemed to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they able to see that you were there watching them carry out the operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 10 of your statement, you describe your return to Kosovo after the fighting with NATO ended, and on the 13th of June you went into Pristina and took over an office that the MUP had been in. You describe seeing a pile of burning documents which you determined, upon inspection, to contain passports and identity documents and application for passports. Were all the names that you saw in the samples you looked at Albanian names?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. All the documents that we looked at, we took several handfuls and asked our interpreter to tell us what they were. This was on our second day in Kosovo, because on the first day we were somewhere else; and on day two, we decided to take over an office to conduct our operations from. This was the Ministry of the Interior buildings and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You took -- you took some photographs of those documents. Did you actually take some samples of the documents you were able to pull out of the pile?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: When we arrived, the whole building was enveloped in smoke; and it make our sort of presence in the building quite unbearable, but we carried on. We tried to identify -- it wasn't hard to identify the source of the smoke because it was -- there was a large pile of paper in sort of an alcove of the building. And it had been burning probably for nearly a day or so. And so we sort of examined it. I took some pictures, maybe three or four pictures, of this burning pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P2504.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How big was this pile of documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I think in my original statement I mentioned it was the size of a truck, but obviously this had burnt down, but it covered a large area between -- from wall -- three walls, three sides of an alcove. Probably the pile was a metre and a half high and as wide as a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see the paragraph on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, it certainly wasn't my intention to take a picture of a vehicle. What I had done is I had taken a number of pictures from the top window, which -- through which I believe the documents had been thrown, and I went downstairs to locate -- take a picture from the road, the pavement, towards the pile of paper, but there was a vehicle parked so it was difficult. But the other pictures would have shown the pile. What you can see is the smoldering, the same smoldering behind the vehicle and to the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you take the pen from the side of the screen there or the usher will assist you, and if you could mark there what you have just talked about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The original picture was taken from a window on the side of the building here, behind these trees or those windows there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've drawn a rectangle and some lines on the upper right-hand corner of the photo.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And I was standing in the road, the main road running through Pristina, the OSCE headquarters would have been off to the right somewhere, and this is the vehicle. And behind it you can see that there is an outline of smoke, which I can assure you is not the smoke of the engine because the engine wasn't running.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were the documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The documents were actually behind, in this area, behind the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You've indicated the document with two sort of half moons --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- on the lower portion of the drawing outside the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This was taken second, third day of our presence in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when had you seen the documents burning initially?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: On the very first time we went to this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the pile was still smoking two days later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It was smoking for days. It was smoldering. It was thick with documents, and that sort of fire doesn't burn very well; it just smolders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you two more photographs while we're on photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit 2506.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who's in this picture.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From left to right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: On the left-hand side the large man is Colonel Kotur; the female is -- was Ms. Babic, my interpreter; myself; and a local Albanian who was able to let us into this property.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where are you standing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm the third from the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. I meant wherefore are you standing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is a house in western Kosovo. Next -- not far, I believe, from some of the villages of Djakovica and that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when, approximately, was this taken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This was probably taken maybe January.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why were you at this location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This was one of my trips with Colonel Kotur. He was taking me around, showing me things. As I said, we had a good relationship; and I was probably the only verifier, besides General DZ, who had access to most units, areas, as long as I was with Colonel Kotur. And he was showing me some of his handy-work, because he had been, I believe, a brigade commander in this area at one time. He knew it well. And the reason he took me to this house, he wanted to show me what happens to a house or property of Albanians who cooperated with the Americans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this was such a house?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This indeed was the house, I believe, where there's -- there are recorded photographs of -- I'm not sure of Chris Hill, but certainly Holbrooke sitting cross-legged smoking a pipe having meetings with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when had that occurred, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, that would have been probably October, before October, thereabout.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we show the witness Exhibit 2506 -- I'm sorry, 2505.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I believe that's the house from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did Colonel Kotur tell you, if anything, how it came to be in that state.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: He told you Maine that the house, following this meeting, they had identified it from the photographs and from local knowledge, and they had come back and they had burnt and blown up the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you when that had happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Not exactly. I can't remember a date, but it would have been shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm finished with that. Next could we show the witness Exhibit 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, when you were proofing with Ms. Carter and I earlier in the week, did you have occasion to review some documents in the nature of military orders dated in late March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me, the Defence objects to the tendering of this evidence through this witness for a very simple reason. As we heard from Mr. Hannis, the witness saw these documents for the first time while he was being proofed for his testimony here, and all those documents pertain to the time -- it's a whole series of documents that I believe my learned colleague would like to show this witness. So these documents, at least at first glance, are documents that were drafted after or created after his tour of duty in Kosovo as a member of the KVM. And these documents are also the kind of documents that he could not have seen or been aware of at the time when he was there. He would not have been aware of what they contained. I think that we cannot establish the minimum level of reliability of the evidence that would be necessary for the Trial Chamber to admit them into evidence. And that is why we would like to object to their tendering into evidence or admission into evidence in this manner. And also it should be noted that these documents have not been signed, have not been sealed, but this is a matter for some other debate. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. These documents, starting with Exhibit Number 1966 through 1969 plus 2015, are -- appear to be documents from the Joint Command regarding military operations proposed in late March 1999. Your Honours, these are documents -- Exhibit 2015 is a document that was a Defence exhibit in the Milosevic case provided by Mr. Milosevic. 1966 through 1969 are documents that we have received pursuant to RFAs to the Serbian authorities. And another document, 1990, which is a MUP staff meeting from February 17th of 1999, was also obtained pursuant to an RFA. The purpose in showing these to the witness was just to have him look at -- well, Your Honours, I have some hesitation about continuing this conversation in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ciaglinski, I'd have to ask you just briefly to leave while we deal with this matter of law and you'll be brought straight back when we finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see the witness is safely out of the room, Your Honour. In his testimony at page -- beginning at page 3222 in the Milosevic case, the witness gave some detailed description of what Colonel Kotur had told him about what the operational plan was going to be to remove the KLA, what areas they were going to be operating in, et cetera. These documents that we received pursuant to RFAs or in the one case that was a Defence exhibit by Mr. Milosevic show orders for military -- a joint military and MUP operations, which we will argue later on in the case line-up in many ways with what Witness Ciaglinski says about what Mr. -- or what Colonel Kotur told him. I don't really need the witness to do that. He's not -- we're not proposing him as a military expert or anything else. It just seemed to be the appropriate time to offer these, and these are things I would tender from the bar table at the conclusion of his testimony. I just wanted to indicate that he had seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He doesn't -- just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, there is no objection to you asking this witness by presenting the terms of the order, as it were, whether that's consistent with a plan that he's describing; but he's not an appropriate vehicle, in our opinion, for introducing these documents. We don't think it appropriate for you to give him the documents, thus giving them some sort of status in the proceedings that's not merited at this moment. And, as you indicate yourself, there are other ways of dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I offered -- I propose to just offer them from the bench and take no comment from him, but it seemed in terms of the chronology of the trial to put them in now when he's talked about Colonel Kotur and I wanted to make the link, but I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if you want to establish consistency between the terms of these and what his understanding of the description of the operation was, then you'll have to do that through oral question and answer. But if you don't think that's necessary, then these can be submitted in some other way at another stage, but not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he testified in Milosevic describing what Colonel Kotur told him about where the operations were going to take place. I can make the argument based on his prior testimony about the documents. I don't need to go through that again with him. I don't think that's the best use of my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we can have the witness. Sorry, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you'll allow me just very briefly. I would like to make a few remarks that may be of some use to us. Quite to the contrary to what my learned colleague is claiming. In his testimony in the Milosevic case, the witness now in court specifically stated that Kotur had not revealed to him any specific plans, nothing that could really take place after the departure of the mission from Kosovo. That's on page 3262 of the testimony of this witness in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the interpretation of the evidence is a matter we can address in later submissions. If Mr. Hannis has overestimated his case at this point, then he'll, no doubt, learn the consequences in due course. Let's have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not going to be necessary to deal with these documents here, Mr. Ciaglinski. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The only other thing I wanted to do with this witness, Your Honour, is number of the other exhibits that were shown to him and discussed by him in his testimony in Milosevic are on our proposed exhibit list. I don't intend to walk him through that again because you can read that in his transcript. But I did want to indicate to the Court the numbers and the transcript page references to those documents. I don't know the most efficient way you would like me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it a long list?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are about 15, 16 documents that have transcript page references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the easiest way is probably to read it into the transcript now and just give us them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Our Exhibit P44 is a map of Kosovo, and that was cited at page 3220 in the Milosevic transcript, and it is Milosevic Exhibit Number 61. Exhibit 395 on our list is Milosevic Exhibit 94 at tab 3 on page 3141, line 6. Our Exhibit 394 is Milosevic 94 at tab 4, also on page 3141. Our Exhibit 677 is Milosevic 94, tab 52, at page 3148. Our Exhibit 623 is Milosevic 96 at page 3156. Our Exhibit 634 is Milosevic 94, tab 63, at page 3181. Our Exhibit 1325 is Milosevic 17 at page 3184. Our 1326 is Milosevic 18, also at 3184. Our Exhibit P1324 is Milosevic 21A and 21B, also at page 3184. Our Exhibit P655 is Milosevic 97 at page 3217. Our Exhibit 2484 is Milosevic 61A at page 2235. Our Exhibit P2238 is Milosevic 98 at page 3252. Our Exhibit 641 is Milosevic 94 at tab 53 on page 3341. Our Exhibit P396, Milosevic 99, at page 3346. And our Exhibit 506, Milosevic 100, at page 3348. And we would tender all these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: Mr. Sainovic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ciaglinski, I have some questions for you, and I would like to first ask you about the work of the commission that you spoke about yesterday and described in your previous statements, where you said that you actually cooperated with the Yugoslav commission for the cooperation with OSCE, and that you met with them quite frequently, and that this commission was, in fact, the official body through which the OSCE commission cooperated with the Yugoslav authorities, if I understood you correctly. Could you please tell me how many meetings were there between the commission -- the Yugoslav commission and your commission in the period between December and March, the period that you can actually testify about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The -- can I just clear one thing up. There was a higher level of commission, of course, in Belgrade itself. That was the top level. Our local Pristina one, we had at least one meeting every single day in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many meetings are we talking about in this period between December and March? If they took place every day, how many of them would be in total?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, exactly the same as the number of days in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many such meetings did you attend of the total number? So there would have been about a hundred meetings. How many out of those hundred meetings did you personally attend?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Probably every one. I might have missed one or two, but the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How would you describe the point of these meetings. These are the meetings where you established the liaison between your commission and the Yugoslav authorities. Am I right when I describe the point of these meetings in these broad terms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The point of the meetings was to pass on any concerns and reports of our activities to your commission and also to hear reactions and complaints or reports from the field from the Yugoslav side also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the point of the meetings was to exchange information. You gave them your information and you asked them your questions, and the Yugoslav side did the same, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did this -- what did this look like in practice? If you had a question, an issue, to raise, request pertaining to some information that pertained to the police, you would then ask this question or make this demand to the liaison officer from the police who attended the meeting. Is that what it looked like? When you had an issue that pertained to the work of the police. This is what I'm specifically interested in.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. The police were not always represented at these meetings. Colonel Mijatovic didn't come every day, not very often, in fact, and so the information was taken by the remainder of the commission, who then would pass on that information to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now just talking about the methodology of your work. I'm not asking you about any specific events. I merely wanted to know what -- how it functioned, and did this also apply to the issues related to the military. If you wanted to know something related to the work of the military, you would ask the representative, the liaison officer, from the Yugoslav army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At those meetings you also presented various requests related to logistics support, accommodation, fuel. You would make those requests to the persons who were there representing the relevant state body in charge of those matters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: If there was no one present to go down to the question, then the commission would direct those questions further, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please focus on what I'm asking you about. If you had a logistics problem, you would present it to one of the persons present there representing the state body in charge of this matter who would be able to resolve that problem. Of course, if that person was not present, then of course it would be forwarded to the relevant person. But if that person was there, you would ask that person. For instance, if you had a visa problem, you would ask it to the representative of the relevant state body dealing with visas. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the issues related to the entry into the country of the commission members, were they also resolved in -- by you putting them to the commission at the commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: If we had difficulties at the border, as we did a few times at Djeneral Jankovic, then we would in fact raise it at this meeting or that could even be written to an ambassadorial level or Ambassador Keller would get straight on to Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you about your impression about the actual powers of this commission. You spoke about that at the Milosevic trial. We know what you said there. Can you now please confirm whether you still state that; in other words, that to your knowledge people present there, members of the commission, and other people who attended those meetings, that those people were not part of the chains of command of the military and the police as far as you knew. When asked specifically by Judge Kwon at the Milosevic trial, you stated that it was absolutely true that these people had not been in the chains of command. This is transcript at page 3271 in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: General Loncar, as a retired general, I can't believe he would have been in the chain of command. Colonel Kotur, as a serving officer, he wasn't commanding anything, to my knowledge, but he had a huge knowledge of the country and the KLA. However, Colonel Mijatovic was in the chain of command --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have to apologise for interrupting you. What I want to know specifically is whether what you said in the Milosevic case, whether you confirmed that today or whether there is a reason for you to change your testimony. There were no dilemmas at that time. At one point your answer was quite unclear, as was your answer just now; and then when the Chamber asked you specifically, you said this -- you made a statement that I just quoted to you. In other words, that the members of the commission were not part of any chains of command. Can you confirm that now? I can read it out to you, if you want me to refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Chamber requires it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ciaglinski, you should continue the answer that you had begun and complete it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On reflection and at the time -- I should say that Colonel Mijatovic - I'll remind you what I said earlier - did not attend all the meetings. Colonel Mijatovic was part of the MUP chain of command; and therefore, except for him, then that is, as I say, he's in the chain of command. When the remainder of the commission arrived, the new commission, General Brankovic and company, they were there for too short a time for me to be able to comment if they were in a chain of command or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know what your position on this really is. So when Judge Kwon asked you: [In English] "Not whether they were.
