General Loncar and some other officials were aware of the fact what was happening at the time, rather, the question was this: Whether they were in the chain of command or not. You can make the answer simpler." [Interpretation] And your answer: [In English] "They were obviously not in the chain of command." [Interpretation] So do you still state that, yes or no? Is this still your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I stick by my comment about the remainder of the commission, but I, on reflection, stick to my point now that Colonel Mijatovic was in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on to some other issues. Do you know who actually sat on the commission of the Yugoslav government for the cooperation with the OSCE; in other words, who were the members of this commission? Could you please give me as many names as you can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this the one in Pristina you're concerned about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm talking about what this witness terms the commission for the cooperation with the OSCE in his testimony and in his -- in the transcript of his previous testimony. Now he is changing his testimony somewhat, but in his statement and in his testimony in the Milosevic case, he is quite clear that there is just one such commission of the Yugoslav government with the cooperation with the OSCE, and this is the commission that I want to ask him about. If he now can share some other insights with us, that would be quite welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So I'm talking about the Yugoslav commission that you speak about in your statement in 2001 and your testimony in the Milosevic case. So my question to you is: Who were the members of that commission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: As I mentioned that I believe that there was a higher level set up in Belgrade; but as I had nothing to do with it on any sort of basis, daily or irregular, I cannot tell you who sat on that commission, except our representative in Belgrade was General Bo Pelmas, and I believe a number of high-level people sat on it from the Serbian side. I've already gone over the people who sat in Kosovo headed by General Loncar, Colonel Mijatovic, Colonel Kotur, there were a number of people from ministries who came and went, whose names I cannot remember so easily. One was a civilian, I think Mr. Petric or Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is why, at least as far as I was able to see from my analysis of your testimony, why you have never mentioned the existence of those various levels, the higher and the lower level, in the commission. Is it true that you have never actually mentioned that, that this -- we hear about this for the first time now in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. I'm somewhat surprised because I speak about what I know, but I believe that others have spoken about what they know. And it has been discussed in their evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, I'm not asking you about what other people said. I'm talking about what you, yourself, have said. You never mentioned any different levels, different compositions of the Yugoslav commission for the cooperation with the OSCE. Very briefly. Is it true that this is the first time that you mentioned this today, although you have had plenty of opportunity to say something about it in the previous occasions. So yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: At my level, the commission I dealt with is the one in Pristina. And to answer the other part of the question: Since no one asked my, I didn't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Petrovic, we will have to break off there, if that's convenient to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That brings our session for today to an end, Mr. Ciaglinski. You will have to resume on Monday, and on Monday we'll be sitting in the afternoon at 2.15. So you need to be back, ready to start your evidence at 2.15. It is important that between now and then you have no discussions with anybody at all about your evidence, that's either what you've said already or what you might yet say in the evidence. Just talk about whatever else you wish, but not the evidence. If you would now, now leave the courtroom with the usher, we'll see you on Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to alert you to a possible scheduling change next week. Subject to my conversation with Defence counsel at the close of this and their estimates on how long cross-examination of this witness will be, we may have a change in the order and I will alert you, through your Legal Officer and through Mr. Haider, of what that is so you don't read too far on something that's not coming up for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 2.15 on Monday.
